more.text: Also called logical controls. Systems and software do the enforcing: firewalls, encryption, antivirus, ACLs, IDS. If a system is doing the work, it's technical.

sides.text: A firewall rule blocks all inbound Telnet. Which control category?

more.text: Technical. The firewall (technology) enforces it. By type it's also preventive.

sides.text: Policies and oversight that govern risk

more.text: Also called administrative controls. They manage risk: policies, risk assessments, security planning, and reviews. They guide the other categories rather than enforce directly.

sides.text: A company writes an acceptable use policy and runs an annual risk assessment.

more.text: Managerial. Policies and risk assessments are management-level governance. The policy itself is also a directive control.

sides.text: Day-to-day security carried out by people

more.text: Performed by people rather than systems: awareness training, following procedures, and day-to-day processes. Compare managerial, which plans and oversees.
Operational. It's people-driven, day-to-day practice. By type it's preventive.
Real-world barriers and monitoring: fences, locks, badge readers, cameras, bollards. They protect people, buildings, and hardware.

sides.text: Badge readers and an access control vestibule guard the server room.

more.text: Physical, and preventive by type. They restrict who can physically reach the equipment.

sides.text: Stops an incident before it happens

more.text: Acts before the event. Examples: firewall rules, MFA, locks, least privilege, hardening. Contrast detective (finds it) and corrective (fixes it).

sides.text: MFA is enabled so stolen passwords alone can't log in.

more.text: Preventive (and technical). It blocks the attack before access is gained.
Works through perception, not force: warning signs, visible cameras, login banners, lighting. It doesn't physically stop anything, which separates it from preventive.

sides.text: Signs warn that the premises are monitored by CCTV and intruders will be prosecuted.

more.text: Deterrent. It discourages by warning; it doesn't physically stop anyone.

sides.text: Finds an incident while or after it happens

more.text: Examples: IDS alerts, log review, audits, CCTV review, SIEM correlation. It reveals what happened but doesn't block it.

sides.text: Security reviews firewall logs and spots a spike in outbound traffic at 3 a.m.

more.text: Detective. Log review identifies suspicious activity but doesn't stop it.

sides.text: Limits damage and restores normal operations

more.text: Applied after an incident to reduce impact and recover: restoring from backup, patching the exploited flaw, quarantining malware, incident response actions.

sides.text: After ransomware hits a file server, admins restore from last night's backup.

more.text: Corrective. Restoring from backup repairs the damage after the incident.

sides.text: Substitute when the main control isn't practical

more.text: Used when the preferred control can't be applied, and it must still meet the original intent. Example: a legacy system that can't be patched is isolated on its own network segment.

sides.text: A medical device can't run antivirus, so it's placed on an isolated VLAN with strict firewall rules.

more.text: Compensating. Segmentation and firewalling stand in for the control (antivirus) that couldn't be used.

sides.text: Tells people what they must do

more.text: Mandates behavior and expectations: policies, standards, procedures, and regulations. They're enforced through consequences rather than technology.

sides.text: A policy states that all laptops must use full-disk encryption.

more.text: Directive (and managerial). The policy mandates the behavior. The encryption itself is a technical control.

sides.text: Category: who implements it. Type: what it does

more.text: Every control has both. A camera is physical (category) and detective (type). A policy is managerial and directive. A firewall rule is technical and preventive.

sides.text: A door lock: which category and which type?

more.text: Physical category, preventive type.

sides.text: Only authorized people can see the data

more.text: Protected by encryption, access controls, and data classification. A confidentiality breach is unauthorized disclosure.

sides.text: An unencrypted laptop holding customer records is stolen.

more.text: Confidentiality is at risk: the data could be read by an unauthorized person. Full-disk encryption would protect it.
Protected by hashing, digital signatures, version control, and access controls. An integrity breach is unauthorized modification.

sides.text: A file's hash no longer matches the published checksum.

more.text: Integrity was compromised: the file was altered or corrupted after the checksum was made.

sides.text: Systems and data are reachable when needed

more.text: Protected by redundancy, backups, failover, and DoS protection. An availability breach is downtime or lost access.

sides.text: A DDoS attack takes the company website offline.

more.text: Availability. Legitimate users can't reach the service.
Proof of origin and action, provided by digital signatures and audit logs. A signed message can't later be disowned by the sender.

sides.text: A vendor claims they never approved an order that carries their digital signature.

more.text: Non-repudiation: the signature, made with their private key, proves they approved it.

sides.text: Compares current state to the target standard

more.text: Identifies the difference between the current security posture and a target (framework, policy, regulation), and what's needed to close it. Used to plan improvements and prepare for audits.

sides.text: Before a PCI DSS audit, a company compares its controls to the standard's requirements.

more.text: Gap analysis. It reveals missing or weak controls that must be fixed to comply.
Verifies identity using something you know, have, or are (and sometimes where you are or what you do). It happens before authorization.

sides.text: A user enters a password, then approves a push notification on their phone.

more.text: Authentication with two factors: something you know and something you have.
Decides which resources and actions an authenticated identity may use. Enforced by permissions, roles, and policies.

sides.text: After logging in, an intern can read the sales report but can't edit it.

more.text: Authorization: access rights granted to an authenticated user.
Tracks and logs activity: logins, resource use, changes. Supports auditing, billing, and investigations. RADIUS and TACACS+ provide AAA.

sides.text: A log shows which admin changed a firewall rule, and when.

more.text: Accounting. It records user activity for auditing and accountability.
Knowledge (password, PIN), possession (token, smart card, phone), inherence (fingerprint, face), location, and behavior. MFA needs factors from different categories.

sides.text: A login requires a password and a security question.

more.text: Not true MFA: both are knowledge factors. MFA needs different categories, such as a password plus a hardware token.

sides.text: Devices prove identity with certificates or keys

more.text: Machines and services authenticate with digital certificates, keys, or tokens, often mutually (mutual TLS). Examples: device certificates, TPM-backed keys, service accounts.

sides.text: Only company-issued laptops with a valid device certificate may join the VPN.

more.text: System authentication. The device proves its identity with a certificate, not a person's password.
Discretionary Access Control. The resource owner sets permissions, typically through ACLs. Flexible but easier to misconfigure. File-system permissions in Windows and Unix work this way.

sides.text: A user shares a document and grants a colleague edit rights.

more.text: DAC. The owner decides access at their discretion.
Mandatory Access Control. A central authority assigns sensitivity labels and clearances, and users can't change them. Used in military and other high-security systems.

sides.text: A user with Secret clearance can't open a Top Secret document, regardless of who wants to share it.

more.text: MAC. Access follows clearance labels set by the system, not owner choice.
Role-Based Access Control. Permissions attach to roles (accountant, help desk) and users inherit them. Simplifies administration and supports least privilege.

sides.text: New hires in accounting automatically get the permissions of the Accountant group.

more.text: RBAC. Permissions come from the job role.

sides.text: Access based on attributes and context

more.text: Attribute-Based Access Control. Decisions combine attributes of the user, resource, and environment: department, device, time, location. Very granular and flexible.

sides.text: Access to records is allowed only for HR staff, on managed devices, during business hours.

more.text: ABAC. It evaluates several attributes (role, device, time) together.
No implicit trust based on network location. Every request is authenticated and authorized with least privilege and continuous verification. It splits into a control plane and a data plane.

sides.text: Employees inside the office network must still authenticate and be authorized for every application.

more.text: Zero trust. Being on the internal network doesn't earn automatic trust.

The zero trust layer where policy is defined and decisions are made. Components: adaptive identity, threat scope reduction, policy-driven access control, the policy administrator, and the policy engine.

sides.text: Which plane contains the policy engine?

more.text: The control plane. It decides; the data plane enforces.
Where decisions are applied. Includes implicit trust zones, the subject/system, and the policy enforcement point that opens or closes the path to a resource.

sides.text: Which plane contains the policy enforcement point?

more.text: The data plane. It enforces what the control plane decided.
Control-plane component that evaluates each access request against policy and context (identity, device health, risk) and decides whether to allow it.

sides.text: A request is checked against identity, device posture, and risk score before access is allowed. Which component decides?

more.text: The policy engine. It makes the decision; the policy administrator carries it out.
Control-plane component that establishes or shuts down the communication path to a resource, such as by issuing a session token, based on the policy engine's decision.

sides.text: Which component sets up the session after the engine approves access?

more.text: The policy administrator. It tells the enforcement point to open or close the path.
Data-plane gateway that enables, monitors, and terminates connections between a subject (user or device) and a system (resource), as directed by the policy administrator.

sides.text: A gateway sits in front of an application and passes only approved traffic. What is it?

more.text: The policy enforcement point (PEP).
Control-plane concept: how strongly to verify depends on context like location, device, and behavior. A login from a new country may trigger an extra verification step.

sides.text: A user logging in from an unfamiliar country is asked for an additional factor.

more.text: Adaptive identity. Verification strength changes with context.

sides.text: Limits what an attacker can reach

more.text: Limits the attack surface and blast radius by restricting access to only what's needed: least privilege, segmentation, narrow policies.

sides.text: Each user can reach only the applications their job requires.

more.text: Threat scope reduction. Less access means less for an attacker to exploit.
Control-plane concept: decisions come from centrally defined policies applied consistently, not ad hoc choices or network location.

sides.text: Access is granted by central rules about who, what, and when, not by which network the user is on.

more.text: Policy-driven access control.
The zone behind the policy enforcement point where traffic is treated as trusted. Zero trust aims to keep this as small as possible.

sides.text: Zero trust tries to shrink which kind of zone?

more.text: The implicit trust zone: where traffic is trusted without further checks.
Short, sturdy posts that block vehicles from reaching buildings or pedestrians. They prevent ram-raid and vehicle attacks.

sides.text: A data center wants to stop a car being driven into its lobby.

more.text: Bollards. They block vehicles physically.

sides.text: Two-door entry that admits one at a time

more.text: Formerly called a mantrap. A small space with two interlocked doors: the second opens only after the first closes and the person is verified. Prevents tailgating and piggybacking.

sides.text: An attacker follows an employee through a door without badging in. What prevents this?

more.text: An access control vestibule. It admits and verifies one person at a time.
Marks and restricts the property boundary. Taller, climb-resistant, or electrified fencing is stronger. It's both deterrent and preventive.

sides.text: Which control defines and restricts the outer perimeter of a site?

more.text: Fencing: a physical barrier that deters and slows intruders.
CCTV deters, and records events for investigation. Can include motion detection. Consider coverage and retention.

sides.text: After a break-in, investigators review recorded footage. What kind of control is this use?

more.text: Detective. Footage reveals what happened. The visible cameras themselves are also deterrent.

sides.text: Human presence to patrol and verify

more.text: Can verify IDs, respond to incidents, and use judgment. Flexible but costly and subject to human error.

sides.text: Which physical control can use judgment to challenge a stranger?

more.text: A security guard. Unlike technology, a person can assess and respond.

sides.text: Card that proves the right to enter

more.text: RFID or smart-card credential for doors and systems, often logged. Can be lost, cloned, or tailgated, so it's often combined with a PIN or biometrics.

sides.text: Door logs show which employees entered the server room and when. Which control provides that?

more.text: Access badges, with readers that log each entry.
Good lighting deters intruders and improves camera footage and guard visibility. Mostly a deterrent.

sides.text: A parking lot is poorly lit. Which physical control helps most?

more.text: Lighting. It deters intruders and makes cameras and guards more effective.
Infrared (heat or motion), pressure (weight on a mat or floor), microwave (reflected waves detect motion), ultrasonic (sound-wave changes detect motion). Used in alarms and monitoring.

sides.text: A mat under a window triggers an alarm when someone steps on it. Which sensor type?

more.text: A pressure sensor. It responds to weight.
A fake system built to look valuable. It detects and studies attackers and wastes their time. Legitimate users have no reason to touch it.

sides.text: A security team deploys a fake database server to see who attacks it.

more.text: A honeypot. It lures attackers so their techniques can be observed.
A decoy network of several honeypots and fake services simulating a real environment, giving a broader view of attacker behavior.

sides.text: A team simulates a whole fake network with several decoy servers.

more.text: A honeynet: multiple honeypots working together.

sides.text: Decoy file that alerts when opened

more.text: A bait file with an attractive name (like Passwords.xlsx) placed on a system. Any access triggers an alert, signaling a possible intruder.

sides.text: A file named Salaries.xlsx on a server alerts the SOC whenever anyone opens it.

more.text: A honeyfile. Opening it signals suspicious access.
Fake credentials, API keys, or records planted to trigger an alert when used. Their use shows someone accessed or stole data they shouldn't have.

sides.text: A fake API key planted in a code repository triggers an alert when it's used.

more.text: A honeytoken. Any use of the fake credential reveals theft.
Changes are requested, reviewed, and approved (often by a change advisory board) before implementation. It prevents unauthorized or untested changes.

sides.text: An admin wants to update a production firewall rule right away. What must happen first?

more.text: The change goes through the approval process: request, review, and sign-off.

sides.text: Who is accountable for the change

more.text: Every system and change has an accountable owner who approves, sponsors, and answers for it.

sides.text: Who is responsible for approving a change to the payroll application?

more.text: The system's owner. Ownership assigns accountability.
Owners, users, IT staff, management, and customers. They should be informed and consulted so impact and timing are understood.

sides.text: A change takes the billing system offline. Who should be consulted?

more.text: Stakeholders, such as the billing team and customers, because they're affected by the downtime.

sides.text: Assess what the change could affect

more.text: Evaluates risk, affected systems, dependencies, downtime, and security effects before the change is made.

sides.text: Before upgrading a database, the team lists every application that depends on it.

more.text: Impact analysis. It identifies what could break.
Changes are tried in a test or staging environment first. Results are documented and reviewed as part of approval.

sides.text: A patch is applied to a staging server before production.

more.text: Testing validates the change; the test results support approval.
Predefined steps to restore the previous state if the change fails: snapshots, backups, rollback scripts. Needed before implementation.

sides.text: An upgrade fails halfway. What should already exist?

more.text: A backout plan, to roll back to the previous working state.
An agreed time, often off-hours, when changes can be made with minimal business impact.

sides.text: Servers are patched only on Sunday at 2 a.m. What is this called?

more.text: A maintenance window.
Written step-by-step instructions that make tasks repeatable and consistent, including how to carry out standard changes.

sides.text: A step-by-step checklist guides every admin through server patching.

more.text: A standard operating procedure (SOP).

sides.text: Allow only approved, or block known bad

more.text: Allow list: only listed items are permitted (stricter). Deny list: listed items are blocked and everything else is allowed. Changes may require updating these lists.

sides.text: A new app must run under application control. What needs updating?

more.text: The allow list, so the new app is permitted.
Activities that must be limited or prohibited during a change, defined in the change scope, so the change stays controlled and conflicts are avoided.

sides.text: During a migration, admins may not make unrelated config changes to the system.

more.text: Restricted activities: limits that keep the change controlled.
Changes can require systems to go offline. Plan the timing, communication, and fallback to limit business impact.

sides.text: A change requires taking the ERP system offline for two hours. What should be planned?

more.text: Downtime: schedule it in a maintenance window and notify stakeholders.
Patches and config changes often need a service or application restart, causing brief disruption. Plan and test for them.

sides.text: A patch takes effect only after the web service restarts.

more.text: A technical implication of change: plan for the restart and its brief disruption.

sides.text: Old systems can break or resist change

more.text: Older apps may not support updates, new protocols, or patches, and can be harmed by changes. Often handled with compensating controls.

sides.text: An unsupported app can't be patched. What's a typical response?

more.text: Apply compensating controls such as isolation, since the change itself isn't possible.

sides.text: Systems that rely on each other

more.text: Changing one component can break others that depend on it. Dependency mapping is part of impact analysis.

sides.text: Updating a library breaks three applications that use it.

more.text: Dependencies. Impact analysis should have identified them.

sides.text: Keep network and system diagrams current

more.text: After changes, update network, data-flow, and architecture diagrams so documentation matches reality and supports troubleshooting and audits.

sides.text: After adding a new VLAN, what documentation should be updated?

more.text: Network diagrams, and related policies and procedures.

sides.text: Keep documents in line with changes

more.text: Policies, SOPs, and baselines must reflect new configurations and processes after a change.

sides.text: A new MFA system is rolled out. What else should change?

more.text: Policies and procedures. Documentation should match the new reality.

sides.text: Track and manage changes over time

more.text: Tracks versions of code, configurations, and documents so changes can be reviewed, compared, and rolled back. Supports accountability and the backout plan.

sides.text: A bad config is pushed. How can the team return to the last good one?

more.text: Version control lets them revert to the previous version.

sides.text: System for issuing and managing certificates

more.text: Public Key Infrastructure: the CAs, certificates, keys, policies, and processes used to create, distribute, validate, and revoke digital certificates.

sides.text: A company must issue and revoke certificates for thousands of devices. What provides the framework?

more.text: PKI.
One half of an asymmetric pair. Anyone can have it. Used to encrypt data for the key owner or verify their signatures.

sides.text: To send a confidential message to Alice with asymmetric encryption, which key do you use?

more.text: Alice's public key. Only her private key can decrypt it.
The secret half of the pair. Decrypts data encrypted with the public key and creates digital signatures. If it's compromised, the key pair can no longer be trusted.

sides.text: Which key creates a digital signature?

more.text: The signer's private key. Others verify it with the public key.

sides.text: Trusted third party holds a copy of keys

more.text: Keys are stored with a trusted party so they can be recovered if lost, or for lawful access. Convenient but a high-value target, so it needs strong protection.

sides.text: An employee leaves and the company needs their encryption keys to recover data. What helps?

more.text: Key escrow. The keys were held by a trusted party.
Everything on the disk is encrypted (BitLocker, FileVault). Protects data at rest if a device is lost or stolen, but not once the OS is unlocked.

sides.text: A laptop is stolen. Which control keeps its data unreadable?

more.text: Full-disk encryption.

sides.text: Encrypts a section or logical drive

more.text: Encrypts a disk partition or logical volume rather than the whole disk, so specific areas, like a data volume, can be protected.

sides.text: Only the data partition holding sensitive files needs to be encrypted.

more.text: Partition (or volume) encryption.
Protects chosen files or folders (like Windows EFS). Fine-grained, but each file must be handled individually and metadata may remain visible.

sides.text: A user needs to encrypt a single sensitive spreadsheet before emailing it.

more.text: File-level encryption.

sides.text: Encrypts the database or its data

more.text: Protects stored data at the database level, for example transparent data encryption (TDE), covering data files, logs, and backups.

sides.text: A company wants the whole database encrypted on disk with no application changes.

more.text: Database encryption, such as transparent data encryption.
Encrypts individual records or columns, such as card numbers, often with separate keys. Most granular, so different users can access different data.

sides.text: Only the credit card column in a customer table needs protection.

more.text: Record- (or column-) level encryption.
Encrypts data as it travels across a network: TLS, HTTPS, IPsec, SSH, VPNs. Prevents eavesdropping and tampering in transit.

sides.text: Customer data crosses the internet between a browser and a web server.

more.text: Transport (communication) encryption, such as TLS.
The same key encrypts and decrypts. Fast, so it's ideal for bulk data (AES). The challenge is sharing the key securely.

sides.text: A 1 GB file needs fast encryption.

more.text: Symmetric encryption, such as AES. It's efficient for large data.
A key pair: public encrypts and private decrypts, or private signs and public verifies. Slower, but it solves key distribution. RSA and ECC are common.

sides.text: Two parties who have never met need to communicate securely.

more.text: Asymmetric encryption, to exchange keys without a pre-shared secret.

sides.text: Safely agreeing on a shared key

more.text: A method to establish a shared symmetric key over an untrusted channel, such as Diffie-Hellman (DH, ECDH). Ephemeral versions provide forward secrecy.

sides.text: Which technique lets two parties derive a shared secret over a public network?

more.text: Key exchange, such as Diffie-Hellman.

sides.text: Common ciphers and what they do

more.text: Symmetric: AES (current standard), 3DES and DES (weak). Asymmetric: RSA, ECC. Hashing: SHA-2 and SHA-3 (MD5 and SHA-1 are weak). Prefer current, well-vetted algorithms.

sides.text: Which is a modern, strong symmetric algorithm: DES, RC4, or AES?

more.text: AES. DES and RC4 are considered weak.

sides.text: Longer keys are harder to brute force

more.text: More bits means more possible keys. AES-256 is stronger than AES-128. RSA needs much longer keys (2048+) than symmetric ciphers for similar strength. ECC reaches strength with shorter keys.

sides.text: Which resists brute force better: AES-128 or AES-256?

more.text: AES-256, because the keyspace is larger.

sides.text: Chip that stores keys on the device

more.text: Trusted Platform Module: tamper-resistant hardware on a motherboard. Stores keys, supports full-disk encryption, and verifies boot integrity.

sides.text: BitLocker keeps its keys in a chip on the motherboard. Which hardware is it?

more.text: A TPM.
Hardware Security Module: a tamper-resistant appliance or card that generates, stores, and uses cryptographic keys and performs crypto operations. Used for CAs and high-assurance key storage.

sides.text: A CA needs its private keys in tamper-resistant hardware that servers can share.

more.text: An HSM.

sides.text: Central control of the key lifecycle

more.text: Handles creation, distribution, rotation, storage, and retirement of keys, often cloud-based. Centralizes control and auditing of keys.

sides.text: A company wants to rotate and audit all encryption keys centrally. What helps?

more.text: A key management system (KMS).
A protected area of a processor, isolated from the main OS, where sensitive data and keys are processed. It helps protect them even if the OS is compromised.

sides.text: Biometric data is processed in an isolated hardware area separate from the OS.

more.text: A secure enclave.
Conceals a message inside another file, such as an image or audio. It hides that communication exists, rather than making it unreadable.

sides.text: Hidden text is discovered inside a photo's pixels.

more.text: Steganography.

sides.text: Replaces data with a meaningless token

more.text: Swaps sensitive data (like a card number) for a random token, with the real value held in a secure vault. Reduces PCI scope. Tokens can't be mathematically reversed.

sides.text: A payment processor stores a random token instead of the real card number.

more.text: Tokenization.
Obscures data by replacing characters (like ****-1234) or substituting realistic fakes. Used for display or test environments.

sides.text: A support agent sees only the last four digits of a card number.

more.text: Data masking.
A fixed-length output that can't be reversed; the same input always gives the same hash. Used to check integrity. It's not encryption: there is no key and nothing to decrypt.

sides.text: A site publishes a checksum so you can verify your download. What's being used?

more.text: A hash. If yours matches, the file hasn't changed.
Makes identical passwords produce different hashes and defeats precomputed rainbow tables. The salt isn't secret and is stored with the hash.

sides.text: Two users with the same password have different stored hashes. Why?

more.text: Salting. A unique random salt was added to each before hashing.

sides.text: A hash signed with the sender's private key

more.text: Verified with the sender's public key. Provides integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation. It doesn't provide confidentiality.

sides.text: Which security goals does a digital signature provide?

more.text: Integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation, but not confidentiality.

sides.text: Slows brute force on weak passwords

more.text: Repeatedly processes a password so each guess is expensive. Algorithms: PBKDF2, bcrypt, scrypt. Defends stored passwords against guessing.

sides.text: A system makes each password guess slower using repeated hashing. What is this?

more.text: Key stretching, such as PBKDF2 or bcrypt.
A distributed ledger where each block contains the previous block's hash, so altering one breaks the chain. Provides integrity and transparency without a central authority.

sides.text: Records are linked by hashes and stored on many nodes, so past entries can't be quietly changed.

more.text: Blockchain.
A transparent record, as in public blockchains, that anyone can inspect and many parties verify. Provides auditability and integrity.

sides.text: Which describes a ledger anyone can read and independently verify?

more.text: An open public ledger, such as Bitcoin's blockchain.
Verifies identities and signs certificates, binding a public key to an identity. Clients trust it through the root of trust.

sides.text: A browser trusts a website's certificate because of who signed it. Who signed it?

more.text: A certificate authority (CA).
Certificate Revocation List: published by the CA, listing certificates that are no longer valid before they expire. Clients download and check it. Can be large and slow.

sides.text: A certificate's private key is stolen. How does the CA tell clients not to trust it?

more.text: It's added to the CRL (or reported through OCSP).
Online Certificate Status Protocol: a client asks a responder whether one certificate is valid. Faster and lighter than downloading a full CRL.

sides.text: A browser asks a server for the status of one certificate in real time.

more.text: OCSP.

sides.text: Signed by itself, not a trusted CA

more.text: Creator and signer are the same, so there's no third-party trust. Free and fine for testing or internal use, but browsers warn about them.

sides.text: A browser shows a warning for a test server's certificate. What's the likely cause?

more.text: It's self-signed, not issued by a trusted CA.
Signed by a publicly trusted CA, so browsers trust it automatically. Needed for public-facing sites.

sides.text: A public website wants visitors' browsers to trust its certificate without warnings.

more.text: A third-party (public CA) certificate.
The trusted anchor of a chain of trust: a root CA certificate, or a hardware root such as a TPM. If it's compromised, everything beneath it is.

sides.text: A certificate chain ends at a trusted, pre-installed root certificate. What is that anchor called?

more.text: The root of trust.

sides.text: Request sent to a CA for a certificate

more.text: Certificate Signing Request: contains the public key and identity details, signed with the private key. The private key itself never leaves your server.

sides.text: Before getting a certificate, a server admin creates a request with the public key and domain name.

more.text: A CSR, which is submitted to the CA.
Covers a domain and its subdomains (*.example.com). Convenient and cheaper, but one compromised key affects every subdomain.

sides.text: A company wants one certificate for mail.example.com and shop.example.com.

more.text: A wildcard certificate (*.example.com).
